title: Two model games: how the plans play out
outcomes: Follows two real Italian Games from the first move to the decision, and says in one sentence what each side was trying to do in each phase
Chooses among three moves at each decision point and gives the reason, checking the choice against the engine and our counts
Names the plan at move 10 in a quiet Giuoco Pianissimo and in a sharp d4-break game
Identifies the slip that decided each game and finds the repair
Describes the pawn structure of each game at move 12 (open and half-open files, pawn islands) and what it suggests
Predicts who stands better from a middlegame position and checks the prediction against the engine and the recorded result

steps.prompt: Before any game: what is White's plan here, and what is Black's? Write one sentence each. You will test your sentences against two real games.

steps.text: **The question.** What does a real Italian Game look like from the first move to the moment that decides it, and which choices decided it? You will watch two games by strong players. In each you will name the plan, choose at the decision points, and find the slip. [I] Model games show typical play, not best play: strong players may deviate, and so may you.

**The quiet Italian.** The family after 3...Bc5 is the Giuoco Piano, 'quiet game'; the version with c3 and d3 is nicknamed Pianissimo, 'very quiet' [R]. White's plan: castle, rook to e1, knight round to f1 and g3, pawn to h3, bishop to b3, pawn to a4. [I] Reasons: c3 prepares d4, d3 guards e4, h3 stops a pin on g4, and the bishop on b3 avoids hits from ...d5 and ...b5. It is slow, but nothing hangs.

steps.text: **What the quiet moves did.** For eight moves White only improved: the rooks stand behind the centre and the pawn on c3 guards d4. Black sent a knight, the king and a pawn toward the kingside, away from the centre. In our data the knight jump to g4 appears in fewer than three games, so Black had left the master track [I]. [H] Waiting is a plan when the other side must commit first. Compare the idea of a prepared break in Nimzowitsch's My System, as on our sheet [S].

steps.text: **How the evaluation moved in Game A.** Engine, White's point of view, single runs at depth 16 and 18, noise about 0.2 of a pawn: move 11, +0.4; move 12, +0.8; move 13 after the capture on g4, +0.7 to +0.9; move 15, +1.6 to +1.7; move 18, about +3. [I] The rise from move 13 to 15 is Black's first slip and from 15 to 18 the second; the quiet opening moves cost Black little.

**What decided Game A.** Two Black slips: the pawn push on move 13 and the knight trade on move 15. Material first: White's strike won a knight for two pawns, yet the engine rated it only about +0.7 to +0.9, because Black had the pawns. [H] The quiet moves created the situation in which one central strike won a piece. Counter-view: the tactic itself was the cause and the quiet moves only set the stage. One game cannot tell these apart.

steps.text: **One possible answer for Game A [I].** Opening: White prepared d4 and kept every piece guarded; Black moved a knight, the king and a pawn to the kingside. Middlegame: White struck in the centre while Black's pieces were away. Decision: the pawn push on move 13 and the knight trade on move 15 let White's edge grow. Your wording will differ.

**How Game A ended.** The header gives 1-0 for White. This lesson does not follow moves 19 to 56, so it does not show how the extra material was converted [V: result only]. Converting an advantage is a separate skill.

steps.text: **What each side wants here.** White holds c3 and d4, and either side can use the open e-file [I]. Black's bishop on b6 and knight on c6 aim at d4. In the earlier chain of d4 and e5, d4 was the base, and Nimzowitsch's chain chapter advises attacking the base (My System, as on our sheet [S]). Now the chain is c3-d4, whose base c3 is hard to reach. [H] Black's pieces can pressure d4 but not win it, while White's bishops stay flexible.

steps.text: **How Game B ended.** The header gives 1-0 for White. This lesson does not follow moves 25 to 39, so the conversion is not shown [V: result only]. What the lesson does show is that the decisive moment came at move 21.

**What decided Game B.** The opening choice cost little: the game move was behind the best by about a quarter-pawn or less (engine runs differ by up to that much) and was rare among masters. In Game B the decisive moment was a Black queen move that left the kingside, which White's queen and bishop then punished [I]. In Game A it was a White central strike. [H] In both, the side that left its king short of defenders was punished; two games prove nothing.

steps.text: **Compare the games.** In Game A the centre stayed closed from move 4 until the break on move 12. In Game B White offered a pawn at move 6 and recaptured it at move 8, so the fight was about the centre from the start. Edward Lasker argued that the pawn skeleton lasts, so arrange the pieces around it (per our sheet [S]). [I] The same question works in both games: which side's pieces can reach the key squares first?

steps.title: The same break, two positions
steps.prompt: Predict, then check: in one position the break d4 is among the engine's best moves, in the other it is not. Which position makes d4 stronger? Only one thing differs: where Black's knight stands.
Look back at your plans from the start of the lesson: did either side follow them? Then name one thing Black could have changed in Game A, one in Game B, and one thing White did that you would copy.

Game B: Black could have brought the knight back instead of moving the queen. White's idea to copy: wait until the enemy pieces have left the centre, then strike. Compare with your first prediction.

steps.text:
**Recap.**
1. [H] From two games: in a quiet Italian, pieces first, break later.
2. [H] In Game A the strike worked with Black's knight on g4 and king on h8; with the knight on f6 the engine preferred quiet moves.
3. [H] A break is ready when your pawn is supported and the enemy pieces are away.
4. A rare move is not a wrong move, but check it.
5. One or two slips decided each middlegame.
6. Name the plan before the move.

steps.prompt: Explain the Italian Game to a beginner in five minutes, using what you saw in the two games. Say the idea, when it works, one example you could set up on a board, and one warning.

steps.text: **One possible five-sentence answer [I].** The Italian aims bishops at f7 and f2 and fights for the centre. Play c3 and d3 and improve your pieces; strike with d4 when the enemy pieces have left the centre. It works when your pawn is supported and no tactic hangs on f2. Example: set up Game A after move 11. Warning: a break at the wrong moment loses a pawn, so test it.

**Self-check.** Did you say when the plan works and when it fails? Did you give an example a beginner could set up on a board? Did you name one mistake and its repair? Did you label anything that is your guess rather than a fact? The app grades nothing here: ask yourself, or ask a friend to listen.
